rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God exposes their former heedlessness; the sudden clarity of what they denied makes their eyesight sharp, a humiliating taunt.
rows.anchor: are meant to humiliate and mock them: today their eyes are very sharp!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scene does not conflict with the verse saying deniers of God's signs will be raised blind; Islahi says their contexts and occasions differ.
rows.anchor: does not contradict the verse which says that those who deny the signs of God will be raised up blind

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some identify the companion as Satan, but Islahi rejects this: Satan would not announce someone in his custody or take responsibility for bringing him; 50:27 shows him disclaiming responsibility.
rows.anchor: Some people are of the view that this refers to the satan which is deputed on every person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companion could be either the driver or the witness mentioned earlier, since either could say the prisoner in his custody is present; Islahi cannot decide definitively.
rows.anchor: Either of the two can be referred to because either of them can utter the words: he who was in my custody is present.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers the driver, because the offender is primarily in his custody and he is responsible for bringing him before God, like a sentinel reporting after duty.
rows.anchor: I am inclined to believe that these words will be uttered by the one who drives on a person.

rows.speaker: Exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally take the dual command as addressed to the driver and witness, a view Islahi finds tenable; the command need not mean they personally throw the offender into Hell.
rows.anchor: understood it to refer to the two angels mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two angels carry out the command by handing the offender to the angels charged with punishment, who cast him into the section reserved for such criminals.
rows.anchor: they will hand over the criminal to the angels who will be entrusted with this task.

rows.speaker: al-Mubarrad
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Arabs sometimes use a dual verb to repeat an imperative, rather than to address two people.
rows.anchor: the view of the famous literary luminary al-Mubarrad that Arabs at times use the dual verb merely to imply repetition of the verb

rows.speaker: al-Mubarrad
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad reads Imru’ al-Qays’s qifā (“wait”) as “Wait! Wait!”, so the poetic address need not be to two companions.
rows.anchor: opinion expressed by al-Mubarrad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi notes that the same directive appears in the plural in Sūrah al-Ḥāqqah, providing a parallel for the command.
rows.anchor: this very directive is given in the plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites al-Mubarrad's proposal as a prompt for further research but is not convinced without satisfactory examples.
rows.anchor: However, I myself am not fully convinced of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For matters of the Hereafter, believers should accept the Qur’an's apparent meaning without pursuing speculative details.
rows.anchor: a believer should profess belief in the apparent meanings of the Qur’ān and should not go after the details.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kaffār means an ingrate and denier; kufr primarily means ingratitude to God and rejection of His rights, while anid denotes an enemy or rival to those rights.
rows.anchor: primarily is used for showing ungratefulness to God and rejection of His rights.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person opposing God's rights is more than merely ungrateful: he is an intense ingrate and an adversary who wants others to reject those rights too.
rows.anchor: he is also a foe and an opponent to these rights so that others too should fulfill them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny and oppose God's rights are also stingy toward fellow humans and try to stop others from fulfilling those rights.
rows.anchor: very stingy in fulfilling the rights of their fellow human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khayr covers virtuous acts generally but commonly means charity toward people.
rows.anchor: very common for the virtue of charity with relation to human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mannāʿ includes both withholding from oneself and obstructing others; the stingy seek to make others stingy so their own behavior is less exposed.
rows.anchor: encompasses the meanings of both to stop one’s self and to stop others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stingy try to make others stingy too, so that their own stinginess will not be exposed.
rows.anchor: they try to make others stingy also so that the secret of their own stinginess is not revealed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A transgressor does more than neglect obligations: he oversteps bounds by taking, or trying to take, what belongs to others.
rows.anchor: they want to transgress bounds and take way or try to take away what others have

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mureeb broadly means one afflicted by doubt, but Qur’anic usage generally concerns doubt about the Day of Judgement, the sūrah’s subject.
rows.anchor: generally used for the doubt a person may have about the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubt about the Judgement is the primary malady behind the listed ingratitude, hostility, stinginess, and transgression.
rows.anchor: the real malady which is the source of all the others is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing shift in style emphatically singles out polytheism as a ruinous root of religious and moral corruption and social disorder.
rows.anchor: at the end with a change in style very emphatically mention polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person who treats another being as God's partner or assumed intercessor may regard belief in the Hereafter as irrelevant and feel free to act after pleasing that being.
rows.anchor: If someone who subscribes to it also believes in the Hereafter, then believing in it or not is equal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When attributes are listed without a conjunction, Islahi says they all coexist in the person described.
rows.anchor: when attributes are mentioned without the particle of conjugation, then it means that all the attributes are simultaneously present

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence moves from derivative traits such as ingratitude and stinginess toward root causes: denial of the Hereafter and polytheism.
rows.anchor: the sequence of their mention progresses from corollaries to principles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second imperative emphatically repeats the earlier order to cast the offender into Hell after listing his traits.
rows.anchor: After that a mention was made of his attributes and then emphatically repeated that he should be thrown

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell has seven gates and multiple sections; the command assigns people with the stated traits to its severe punishment.
rows.anchor: Hell has seven gates and many sections.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the criminals enter Hell, each blames Satan, who is assigned under God's established practice to those heedless of His remembrance; Satan disclaims making the man rebellious.
rows.anchor: every inhabitant of Hell will blame Satan for his error and misguidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's denial does not mean he denies calling people toward error; 14:22 says he admits making false promises and calling, while people chose to respond without compulsion.
rows.anchor: This statement of Satan does not mean that he will refute his act of calling people towards error.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying the man had gone far astray means he was so distant from truth that he no longer sought guidance, making him vulnerable to Satan under God's practice.
rows.anchor: there was no chance for him to return to the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Misleading leaders likewise absolve themselves; 14:21 depicts the weak asking their powerful leaders for protection, and the leaders saying they would have guided them if God had.
rows.anchor: in a similar manner leaders who led people astray will absolve themselves from their responsibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God ends the dispute: arguing and blaming one another cannot erase anyone's responsibility because He warned them beforehand.
rows.anchor: there is no use fighting in His presence. This blame-game cannot absolve anyone of his responsibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning began after Satan challenged God that he would mislead most of Adam's descendants; God permitted his efforts but warned that Satan and his human and jinn followers would enter Hell.
rows.anchor: right after Satan had challenged Him that if given respite he will lead the majority of Adam’s progeny astray.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God continued sending prophets and messengers to teach guidance and the fate of Satan's followers, leaving people no excuse for rejecting truth.
rows.anchor: kept on sending His prophets and messengers who at various intervals continued to inform people of God’s guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's prior word cannot be changed by complaints; His promises and threats are certain, and the punished are receiving what they earned.
rows.anchor: The promises and threats of God are absolutely certain and unassailable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They reap what they sow; God does not wrong His servants even slightly.
rows.anchor: They are reaping only what they had sown. So they should now taste it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A negative statement using an intensive form intensifies the negation, so the meaning is that God is not the slightest unjust to His servants.
rows.anchor: when an exaggerated statement is expressed in the negative, then the purpose is to exaggerate the negation.

rows.speaker: exegetes and translators
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the common rendering “He is not unjust” as too weak: the emphatic wording means not the slightest unjust, and translators generally follow the weaker gloss.
rows.anchor: they interpret it to mean (He is not unjust). Most translators follow this interpretation while translating the verse
